title: Enthalpy, Entropy and Non-Equilibrium Reactions | Year 12 Chemistry
description:
Explain why burning glucose and photosynthesis stay away from equilibrium, using the signs of the enthalpy change and the entropy change. Read the sign of the Gibbs free energy change (delta G) to decide whether a reaction is favoured, and keep that separate from how fast it runs. Work through the glucose example one step at a time, then compare the reverse process, photosynthesis.

Chemistry 2017: Year 12 Module 5, Equilibrium and Acid Reactions. Supports analysing non-equilibrium systems in terms of the effect of entropy and enthalpy.
Syllabus dotpoint (NSW Chemistry Stage 6, 2017, Module 5):
"analyse examples of non-equilibrium systems in terms of the effect of entropy and enthalpy, for example:
- combustion reactions
- photosynthesis"
Official 2017 course: https://www.nsw.gov.au/education-and-training/nesa/curriculum/science/chemistry-stage-6-2017

Prerequisite: Dynamic equilibrium in a closed system, exothermic and endothermic reactions, entropy as the spread of particles and energy, and the link between enthalpy, entropy and delta G. Next: What a flask already at equilibrium does when it is disturbed by a change in concentration or temperature.

#Year12Chemistry #Entropy #HSCScience
syllabusDotpoints:
analyse examples of non-equilibrium systems in terms of the effect of entropy and enthalpy, for example:
- combustion reactions
- photosynthesis

title: Squeezing a Gas Equilibrium: Predicting the Shift | Year 12 Chemistry
description:
Squeeze a gas mixture that is sitting at equilibrium and predict which way it shifts by counting only the gas particles. Explain the shift as the side with fewer gas particles becoming favoured when every gas is more crowded. Handle equal gas counts and solids, and tell a squeeze apart from adding an inert gas at fixed volume.

Chemistry 2017: Year 12 Module 5, Equilibrium and Acid Reactions. Supports explaining how pressure and volume changes affect an equilibrium, using Le Chatelier’s principle and collision theory.
Syllabus dotpoint (NSW Chemistry Stage 6, 2017, Module 5):
"investigate the effects of temperature, concentration, volume and/or pressure on a system at equilibrium and explain how Le Chatelier’s principle can be used to predict such effects"
"explain the overall observations about equilibrium in terms of the collision theory"
Official 2017 course: https://www.nsw.gov.au/education-and-training/nesa/curriculum/science/chemistry-stage-6-2017

Prerequisite: Le Chatelier’s principle for concentration and temperature changes, why a disturbance is only partly cancelled, and gas pressure as particles hitting the walls (Year 11). Next: Catalysts and equilibrium, a faster route to the same mixture.

#Year12Chemistry #Equilibrium #HSCScience
syllabusDotpoints: investigate the effects of temperature, concentration, volume and/or pressure on a system at equilibrium and explain how Le Chatelier’s principle can be used to predict such effects

title: Catalysts and Equilibrium: Same Mixture, Sooner | Year 12 Chemistry
description:
A catalyst makes a reaction faster, so why does it not give more product at equilibrium? Explain a catalyst as an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy that speeds up both the forward and reverse reactions. Distinguish the product formed in a limited time from the amount present at equilibrium, and state what a catalyst does to a mixture that is already at equilibrium.

Chemistry 2017: Year 12 Module 5, Equilibrium and Acid Reactions. Supports explaining that a catalyst changes how soon equilibrium is reached, not where it sits, using collision theory and activation energy.
Syllabus dotpoint (NSW Chemistry Stage 6, 2017, Module 5):
"examine how activation energy and heat of reaction affect the position of equilibrium"
"explain the overall observations about equilibrium in terms of the collision theory"
Official 2017 course: https://www.nsw.gov.au/education-and-training/nesa/curriculum/science/chemistry-stage-6-2017

Prerequisite: Squeezing a gas mixture and how the forward and reverse rates change by different factors, plus collisions that have enough energy to react. Next: Writing the equilibrium constant, K, from a balanced equation.

#Year12Chemistry #Catalysts #HSCScience
syllabusDotpoints: examine how activation energy and heat of reaction affect the position of equilibrium
explain the overall observations about equilibrium in terms of the collision theory

title: The Equilibrium Constant, K: Writing Expressions | Year 12 Chemistry
description:
When a settled mixture changes all of its amounts, the ratio of concentrations stays the same at a fixed temperature. Name that ratio K and write its expression for a reaction in solution from a balanced equation, using coefficients as powers and leaving out solids and pure liquids. Read whether a stated K is large, small or middling for that reaction.

Chemistry 2017: Year 12 Module 5, Equilibrium and Acid Reactions. Supports deducing equilibrium expressions for homogeneous reactions in solution.
Syllabus dotpoint (NSW Chemistry Stage 6, 2017, Module 5):
"deduce the equilibrium expression (in terms of Keq) for homogeneous reactions occurring in solution"
Official 2017 course: https://www.nsw.gov.au/education-and-training/nesa/curriculum/science/chemistry-stage-6-2017

Prerequisite: Dynamic equilibrium with equal non-zero rates, the settled mixtures from the earlier flask and tube examples, and concentration as moles per litre. Next: Calculating K and equilibrium concentrations with an ICE table.

#Year12Chemistry #Keq #HSCScience
syllabusDotpoints: deduce the equilibrium expression (in terms of Keq) for homogeneous reactions occurring in solution

title: Calculating K and Equilibrium Concentrations | Year 12 Chemistry
description:
Build an ICE table (initial, change, equilibrium) to calculate K from a starting mixture and one measured equilibrium value, then check the answer. Use K to find equilibrium concentrations in a simple case where the algebra comes out as a perfect square. Explain how K changes when an equation is reversed.

Chemistry 2017: Year 12 Module 5, Equilibrium and Acid Reactions. Supports performing calculations to find Keq and the concentrations of substances in an equilibrium system.
Syllabus dotpoint (NSW Chemistry Stage 6, 2017, Module 5):
"perform calculations to find the value of Keq and concentrations of substances within an equilibrium system"
Official 2017 course: https://www.nsw.gov.au/education-and-training/nesa/curriculum/science/chemistry-stage-6-2017

Prerequisite: Writing equilibrium expressions and the meaning of K, the size of K, and concentration as moles per litre from a balanced equation. Next: Why factories do not wait for equilibrium, and why they choose compromise conditions.

#Year12Chemistry #Keq #HSCScience
syllabusDotpoints: perform calculations to find the value of Keq and concentrations of substances within an equilibrium system

title: Industrial Equilibrium: Why Factories Compromise | Year 12 Chemistry
description:
Why do factories choose conditions that do not give the highest equilibrium yield? Explain the difference between the equilibrium yield (where the mixture settles) and the rate (how soon it gets there), then justify a temperature, pressure, catalyst and product-removal choice for an industrial reaction that gives out heat and produces fewer gas particles. Explain why a plant removes product and recycles what is left over.

Chemistry 2017: Year 12 Module 5, Equilibrium and Acid Reactions. Supports explaining and predicting temperature and pressure effects using Le Chatelier’s principle, with heat of reaction and activation energy.
Syllabus dotpoint (NSW Chemistry Stage 6, 2017, Module 5):
"investigate the effects of temperature, concentration, volume and/or pressure on a system at equilibrium and explain how Le Chatelier’s principle can be used to predict such effects"
"examine how activation energy and heat of reaction affect the position of equilibrium"
Official 2017 course: https://www.nsw.gov.au/education-and-training/nesa/curriculum/science/chemistry-stage-6-2017

Prerequisite: Le Chatelier’s principle, catalysts that change the rate but not the destination, and the size of K from the earlier calculation videos. Next: Reading unfamiliar equilibrium graphs.

#Year12Chemistry #Industry #HSCScience
syllabusDotpoints: investigate the effects of temperature, concentration, volume and/or pressure on a system at equilibrium and explain how Le Chatelier’s principle can be used to predict such effects
examine how activation energy and heat of reaction affect the position of equilibrium

title: Reaction Quotient Q: Predicting the Direction | Year 12 Chemistry
description:
Given a mixture that has not settled, and the K for that temperature, decide which way it will run before anything changes. Write the reaction quotient, Q, from supplied concentrations, compare Q with K, and state the direction and the reason. Then use the same steps on an unseen mixture.

Chemistry 2017: Year 12 Module 5, Equilibrium and Acid Reactions. Supports using equilibrium quantities and constants to predict the direction in which a reaction may proceed.
Syllabus dotpoint (NSW Chemistry Stage 6, 2017, Module 5):
"perform calculations to find the value of Keq and concentrations of substances within an equilibrium system, and use these values to make predictions on the direction in which a reaction may proceed"
Official 2017 course: https://www.nsw.gov.au/education-and-training/nesa/curriculum/science/chemistry-stage-6-2017

Prerequisite: Calculating K from settled concentrations, the K expression and its rules, and concentration in mol/L. Next: Harder ICE table and reaction quotient decisions.

#Year12Chemistry #Equilibrium #HSCScience
syllabusDotpoints: perform calculations to find the value of Keq and concentrations of substances within an equilibrium system, and use these values to make predictions on the direction in which a reaction may proceed

title: Flowering Plant Reproduction: Pollination to Seed | Year 12 Biology
description:
Sequence reproduction in flowering plants from pollination to seed, and explain why pollination is not yet fertilisation. Explain how a pollen tube carries sperm to the egg. Name vegetative propagation as the asexual route in plants, then match each route to the conditions where it works best.

Biology 2017: Year 12 Module 5, Heredity. Supports analysing sexual and asexual reproduction in plants.
Syllabus dotpoint (NSW Biology Stage 6, 2017, Module 5):
"explain the mechanisms of reproduction that ensure the continuity of a species, by analysing sexual and asexual methods of reproduction in a variety of organisms, including but not limited to:
- plants: asexual and sexual reproduction"
Official 2017 course: https://www.nsw.gov.au/education-and-training/nesa/curriculum/science/biology-stage-6-2017

Prerequisite: Sexual and asexual reproduction, gametes joining at fertilisation, clones, and the conditions that favour clones or variety. Next: Reproduction without flowers or seeds: yeast, bacteria and protists.

#Year12Biology #Reproduction #HSCScience
syllabusDotpoints:
explain the mechanisms of reproduction that ensure the continuity of a species, by analysing sexual and asexual methods of reproduction in a variety of organisms, including but not limited to:
- plants: asexual and sexual reproduction

title: Human Pregnancy: Fertilisation to Implantation | Year 12 Biology
description:
Trace a human pregnancy from fertilisation in the oviduct, through cleavage and the blastocyst, to implantation in a uterine lining that progesterone has prepared. Explain why the embryo’s hCG keeps the corpus luteum making progesterone, and why the placenta takes over progesterone over the first two to three months. Separate hCG from progesterone, and an embryo from a fetus.

Biology 2017: Year 12 Module 5, Heredity. Supports analysing fertilisation, implantation and the hormonal control of pregnancy in mammals.
Syllabus dotpoint (NSW Biology Stage 6, 2017, Module 5):
"analyse the features of fertilisation, implantation and hormonal control of pregnancy and birth in mammals"
Official 2017 course: https://www.nsw.gov.au/education-and-training/nesa/curriculum/science/biology-stage-6-2017

Prerequisite: Sexual reproduction in animals, one set of chromosomes in each gamete, and internal fertilisation with few young. Next: How pregnancy hormone loops hold a pregnancy steady, and how labour builds.

#Year12Biology #Pregnancy #HSCScience
syllabusDotpoints: analyse the features of fertilisation, implantation and hormonal control of pregnancy and birth in mammals

title: Pregnancy Feedback and Labour: Hormone Loops | Year 12 Biology
description:
Explain how a pregnancy stays steady for nine months, and why no new egg is released during it. Use negative feedback, where progesterone turns down the pituitary hormones FSH and LH, to explain why ovulation stops. Explain how labour builds through positive feedback involving oxytocin and the cervix, and how prolactin and oxytocin help make and release milk.

Biology 2017: Year 12 Module 5, Heredity. Supports analysing the hormonal control of pregnancy and birth in mammals, including negative and positive feedback.
Syllabus dotpoint (NSW Biology Stage 6, 2017, Module 5):
"analyse the features of fertilisation, implantation and hormonal control of pregnancy and birth in mammals"
Official 2017 course: https://www.nsw.gov.au/education-and-training/nesa/curriculum/science/biology-stage-6-2017

Prerequisite: Human pregnancy from fertilisation to implantation, including hCG, progesterone and the placenta, and that a hormone is a messenger carried by the blood. Next: How farmers use reproduction knowledge to breed animals and crops.

#Year12Biology #Pregnancy #HSCScience
syllabusDotpoints: analyse the features of fertilisation, implantation and hormonal control of pregnancy and birth in mammals

title: Breeding Animals and Crops: Methods and Costs | Year 12 Biology
description:
Explain how artificial insemination and artificial pollination let farmers choose parents for animals and crops, and which reproduction knowledge each method depends on. Explain why copying a winning animal or plant gives a uniform crop and a shared weakness. Evaluate the gain, the loss of variety and the cost of these methods, using criteria a judge would weigh.

Biology 2017: Year 12 Module 5, Heredity. Supports evaluating the impact of scientific knowledge on the manipulation of plant and animal reproduction in agriculture.
Syllabus dotpoint (NSW Biology Stage 6, 2017, Module 5):
"evaluate the impact of scientific knowledge on the manipulation of plant and animal reproduction in agriculture"
Official 2017 course: https://www.nsw.gov.au/education-and-training/nesa/curriculum/science/biology-stage-6-2017

Prerequisite: Clones, alleles and variation, how pollination and fertilisation work in plants, and how sperm reaches an egg in animals. Next: How DNA is copied accurately while its information is kept.

#Year12Biology #Agriculture #HSCScience
syllabusDotpoints: evaluate the impact of scientific knowledge on the manipulation of plant and animal reproduction in agriculture

title: How DNA Is Copied: Base Pairing and Replication | Year 12 Biology
description:
Explain how a cell copies billions of DNA letters almost without error. Name the parts of a DNA nucleotide, pair A with T and C with G, and explain why one strand acts as a template for the other. Trace a short molecule through semi-conservative replication, where each new molecule keeps one original strand, and explain why copying errors are rare.

Biology 2017: Year 12 Module 5, Heredity. Supports modelling DNA replication using the Watson and Crick model, including nucleotide composition, pairing and bonding.
Syllabus dotpoint (NSW Biology Stage 6, 2017, Module 5):
"model the processes involved in cell replication, including but not limited to:
- DNA replication using the Watson and Crick DNA model, including nucleotide composition, pairing and bonding"
Official 2017 course: https://www.nsw.gov.au/education-and-training/nesa/curriculum/science/biology-stage-6-2017

Prerequisite: DNA as inherited information, genes, alleles and copying errors, and how a single cell copies its DNA before it splits. Next: Mitosis, how a cell shares its copied chromosomes between two new cells.

#Year12Biology #DNA #HSCScience
syllabusDotpoints:
model the processes involved in cell replication, including but not limited to:
- DNA replication using the Watson and Crick DNA model, including nucleotide composition, pairing and bonding

title: Mitosis: How Each New Cell Keeps Every Chromosome | Year 12 Biology
description:
Explain why a cell copies its DNA before it divides, and what a copied chromosome looks like. Count chromosomes by counting centromeres, then name the four stages of mitosis in order and say what happens to the chromosomes in each. Track chromosome numbers through a model cell and a human cell to show why both new cells keep every chromosome.

Biology 2017: Year 12 Module 5, Heredity. Supports modelling mitosis as a cell-replication process, including the four stages in order.
Syllabus dotpoint (NSW Biology Stage 6, 2017, Module 5):
"model the processes involved in cell replication, including but not limited to:
- mitosis and meiosis"
Official 2017 course: https://www.nsw.gov.au/education-and-training/nesa/curriculum/science/biology-stage-6-2017

Prerequisite: Chromosomes as structures that hold DNA, gametes carrying one set, and DNA copying before a cell splits. Next: Meiosis, how a cell ends up with one set of chromosomes to make gametes.

#Year12Biology #Mitosis #HSCScience
syllabusDotpoints:
model the processes involved in cell replication, including but not limited to:
- mitosis and meiosis

title: Meiosis: Halving Chromosome Sets for Gametes | Year 12 Biology
description:
Explain why gametes must be haploid, and how meiosis makes four haploid cells from one diploid cell with one copying and two divisions. Describe what happens in prophase I, metaphase I, anaphase I and meiosis II. Explain why crossing over and independent assortment make new combinations of existing alleles, but not new alleles.

Biology 2017: Year 12 Module 5, Heredity. Supports modelling meiosis as a cell-replication process and the formation of new combinations of genotypes.
Syllabus dotpoint (NSW Biology Stage 6, 2017, Module 5):
"model the processes involved in cell replication, including but not limited to:
- mitosis and meiosis"
"model the formation of new combinations of genotypes produced during meiosis"
Official 2017 course: https://www.nsw.gov.au/education-and-training/nesa/curriculum/science/biology-stage-6-2017

Prerequisite: Mitosis, homologous pairs, diploid and haploid cells, chromatids and centromeres, and alleles as versions of a gene. Next: DNA in prokaryotes and eukaryotes, and how it is arranged in different kinds of cell.

#Year12Biology #Meiosis #HSCScience
syllabusDotpoints:
model the processes involved in cell replication, including but not limited to:
- mitosis and meiosis
model the formation of new combinations of genotypes produced during meiosis

title: Calculating K: the Three Question Types and ICE Tables | Year 12 Chemistry
description:
Equilibrium calculation questions come in three types. Do the first two here: substitute settled concentrations straight into K, then use an ICE table (I for initial, C for change, E for equilibrium) when you are given a start and one measured equilibrium value. Put the measured value in the equilibrium row first, work out its change as equilibrium minus initial, then use the coefficients for the other changes. Also see how K flips when the equation is written backwards.

Chemistry 2017: Year 12 Module 5, Equilibrium and Acid Reactions. Supports performing calculations to find Keq and the concentrations of substances in an equilibrium system.
Syllabus dotpoint (NSW Chemistry Stage 6, 2017, Module 5):
"perform calculations to find the value of Keq and concentrations of substances within an equilibrium system"
Official 2017 course: https://www.nsw.gov.au/education-and-training/nesa/curriculum/science/chemistry-stage-6-2017

Prerequisite: Writing equilibrium expressions and the meaning of K. Next: Finding equilibrium concentrations from K, with no quadratic needed.

#Year12Chemistry #Keq #HSCScience
syllabusDotpoints: perform calculations to find the value of Keq and concentrations of substances within an equilibrium system

title: Temperature and the Equilibrium Constant: How Does Heat Change K? | Year 12 Chemistry
description:
Adding a chemical, squeezing the container or adding a catalyst never changes K. Changing the temperature does. See why with a sealed tube of brown nitrogen dioxide: heating speeds up both reactions, but the one that takes in heat speeds up more, so the mixture settles somewhere new and K changes. Learn the rule for endothermic and exothermic reactions, and how to read it backwards from a table of K values.

Chemistry 2017: Year 12 Module 5, Equilibrium and Acid Reactions. Supports explaining the effect of temperature on Keq.
Syllabus dotpoint (NSW Chemistry Stage 6, 2017, Module 5):
"explain the effect of changes of temperature on values of Keq for exothermic and endothermic reactions"
Official 2017 course: https://www.nsw.gov.au/education-and-training/nesa/curriculum/science/chemistry-stage-6-2017

Prerequisite: K and the reaction quotient Q, and Le Chatelier's principle. Next: Finding K from a colour reading (colourimetry).

#Year12Chemistry #Keq #HSCScience
syllabusDotpoints: explain the effect of changes of temperature on values of Keq for exothermic and endothermic reactions
